records.source: וַיִּסְע֖וּ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַֽיַּחֲנוּ֙ בְּעַֽרְב֣וֹת מוֹאָ֔ב מֵעֵ֖בֶר לְיַרְדֵּ֥ן יְרֵחֽוֹ׃ס
records.gloss: And set out [the] sons of Israel and camped in [the] plains of Moab, beyond [the] Jordan [at] Jericho.
pieces: Then the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} moved on and camped in the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho.

L.1: And the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel set out and camped in the plains of Moab, across the Jordan [from] Jericho.

R.1: Then the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} moved on. They set up camp on the flat land of Moab, across the Jordan River from the city of Jericho.

decisions.choice: the plains of Moab: the low land east of the Jordan, just north of the Dead Sea
decisions.reason: This is Israel's last camp before they cross into Canaan. They are still here at the end of the book (33:48-50; 36:13), and Moses dies on a mountain above it (Deuteronomy 34:1, 8). The land had belonged to Moab before Sihon the Amorite took it from them (21:26).

decisions.choice: across the Jordan from Jericho: on the east bank, facing Jericho on the west
decisions.reason: "Beyond the Jordan" is said from the point of view of the land west of the river, the land Israel is about to enter. Jericho lies on the other side of the river from the camp; it is the first town Israel will take (Joshua 6).

decisions.choice: the flat land of Moab, the Jordan River, the city of Jericho
decisions.reason: Readable explains "plains" and says what the Jordan and Jericho are, for readers who do not know the places.

records.heading: Israel camps in the plains of Moab

records.source: וַיַּ֥רְא בָּלָ֖ק בֶּן־צִפּ֑וֹר אֵ֛ת כָּל־אֲשֶׁר־עָשָׂ֥ה יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לָֽאֱמֹרִֽי׃
records.gloss: And saw Balak son of Zippor all that had done Israel to the Amorite[s].
pieces: Balak son of Zippor saw everything that Israel had done to the Amorites.

L.2: And Balak son of Zippor saw all that Israel had done to the Amorites.

R.2: Balak son of Zippor had seen all that Israel had done to the Amorites.

decisions.choice: all that Israel had done to the Amorites: the defeat of Sihon and Og
decisions.reason: Israel had just defeated Sihon king of the Amorites and taken his towns, and then Og king of Bashan (21:21-35). Both are called "the two kings of the Amorites" (Deuteronomy 3:8). Their lands lay on Moab's northern border, so Balak had watched it happen close by.

decisions.choice: Balak son of Zippor: a king of Moab known from this story
decisions.reason: The narrator names Balak first and says only in verse 4 that he was king of Moab. Later Scripture remembers him for hiring Balaam against Israel (Joshua 24:9; Judges 11:25; Micah 6:5).

records.heading: Balak sends for Balaam

records.source: וַיָּ֨גָר מוֹאָ֜ב מִפְּנֵ֥י הָעָ֛ם מְאֹ֖ד כִּ֣י רַב־ה֑וּא וַיָּ֣קָץ מוֹאָ֔ב מִפְּנֵ֖י בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃
records.gloss: And was afraid Moab from before the people exceedingly, for numerous [was] it; and felt dread Moab before [the] sons of Israel.
pieces: Moab was terrified of the people, because there were so many of them; Moab felt a sickening dread of the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}}.

L.3: And Moab was greatly afraid of the people, for it [was] numerous; and Moab felt dread before the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel.

R.3: The people of Moab were terrified, because the Israelites were so many. They felt sick with fear of them.

decisions.choice: felt dread: a sickened fear, close to loathing
decisions.reason: The second verb is stronger than the first. It is the word used of the Egyptians, who "dreaded" the Israelites as their numbers grew (Exodus 1:12). Moab now feels what Egypt felt, and for the same reason: there are so many of them.

decisions.choice: Moab: the nation, spoken of as one person
decisions.reason: The verbs are singular: Moab the nation is afraid, as one body, as "Israel" is in verse 2.

decisions.choice: The people of Moab
decisions.reason: Readable says "the people of Moab" so that the reader does not take Moab for a single man.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר מוֹאָ֜ב אֶל־זִקְנֵ֣י מִדְיָ֗ן עַתָּ֞ה יְלַחֲכ֤וּ הַקָּהָל֙ אֶת־כָּל־סְבִ֣יבֹתֵ֔ינוּ כִּלְחֹ֣ךְ הַשּׁ֔וֹר אֵ֖ת יֶ֣רֶק הַשָּׂדֶ֑ה וּבָלָ֧ק בֶּן־צִפּ֛וֹר מֶ֥לֶךְ לְמוֹאָ֖ב בָּעֵ֥ת הַהִֽוא׃
records.gloss: And said Moab to [the] elders of Midian, now will lick up the assembly all around us, as licks up the ox [the] green of the field. And Balak son of Zippor [was] king of Moab at the time, that [one].
pieces: So Moab said to the elders of Midian, "Now this assembly will lick up everything around us, as an ox crops the grass of a field." Balak son of Zippor was king of Moab at that time.

L.4: And Moab said to the elders of Midian, "Now the assembly will lick up all that is around us, as the ox licks up the green growth of the field." And Balak son of Zippor [was] king of Moab at that time.

R.4: The Moabites said to the elders of Midian, "This crowd will soon eat up everything around us, as an ox eats up the grass in a field." At that time Balak son of Zippor was the king of Moab.

decisions.choice: the elders of Midian: the leaders of a people allied with Moab
decisions.reason: Midian was a people of tribes and clans, led by elders and chiefs (31:8). Moses' wife was a Midianite (Exodus 2:16-21). Here Midian joins Moab against Israel; Midianite women take part in leading Israel astray in chapter 25, and Israel's war against Midian in chapter 31 ends with Balaam's death (31:8, 16).

decisions.choice: lick up as the ox licks up the grass: use up the land completely
decisions.reason: An ox grazing strips a field bare. Moab fears that Israel will consume everything around it, as it had just taken the land of the Amorites (21:24-25). The picture comes from a people of herdsmen.

decisions.choice: Balak ... was king of Moab at that time: background given in passing
decisions.reason: The narrator pauses to say who Balak is before he acts in verse 5.

decisions.choice: assembly (L, B), crowd (R)
decisions.reason: The word usually names Israel gathered as a people (as in 20:4). Here Moab uses it for Israel as a great mass of people, so Readable says "crowd".

records.source: וַיִּשְׁלַ֨ח מַלְאָכִ֜ים אֶל־בִּלְעָ֣ם בֶּן־בְּע֗וֹר פְּ֠תוֹרָה אֲשֶׁ֧ר עַל־הַנָּהָ֛ר אֶ֥רֶץ בְּנֵי־עַמּ֖וֹ לִקְרֹא־ל֑וֹ לֵאמֹ֗ר הִ֠נֵּה עַ֣ם יָצָ֤א מִמִּצְרַ֨יִם֙ הִנֵּ֤ה כִסָּה֙ אֶת־עֵ֣ין הָאָ֔רֶץ וְה֥וּא יֹשֵׁ֖ב מִמֻּלִֽי׃
records.gloss: And he sent messengers to Balaam son of Beor, to Pethor, which [is] by the River, [the] land of [the] sons of his people, to call him, saying, look, a people has come out from Egypt; look, it has covered the eye of the land, and it [is] dwelling opposite me.
pieces: He sent messengers to call Balaam son of Beor at Pethor, near the River, in the land of his own people. The message said, "A people has come out of Egypt. They are covering the face of the land, and they have settled right across from me.

L.5: And he sent messengers to Balaam son of Beor at Pethor, which [is] by the River, [in the] land of the {{gender:children|sons}} of his people, to call him, saying, "Look, a people has come out of Egypt. Look, it has covered the eye of the land, and it is dwelling opposite me.

R.5: So Balak sent messengers to Balaam son of Beor. Balaam lived in the town of Pethor, near the Euphrates River, in the land of his own people. Balak wanted Balaam to come to him. His message said, "A whole nation has come out of Egypt. They cover the land, and they are living right next to me.

decisions.choice: Balaam son of Beor: a famous seer from far away
decisions.reason: Balaam is a man people sent for to bless or to curse (verse 6). Later Scripture remembers him as a diviner (Joshua 13:22) who was hired against Israel (Deuteronomy 23:5; Nehemiah 13:2). A wall inscription found at Deir Alla in Jordan, written some centuries later, speaks of "Balaam son of Beor" as a seer of the gods, so his name was known outside Israel too.

decisions.choice: the River: the Euphrates
decisions.reason: "The River" with no other name usually means the Euphrates (Genesis 31:21; Exodus 23:31). Deuteronomy 23:5 places Pethor in Aram-naharaim, "Aram of the two rivers", in upper Mesopotamia, and Balaam says he came "from Aram" (23:7). It was a journey of many days from Moab.

decisions.choice: the land of the sons of his people: Balaam's homeland
alternatives: the land of the sons of Ammon
decisions.reason: The Hebrew text reads "his people" ('ammo). The Samaritan Pentateuch, the Syriac and the Latin Vulgate read "Ammon", a very similar word, which would put Balaam close to Moab. The Hebrew reading fits "the River" and Aram (23:7) and is kept. Reviewers should check the evidence.

decisions.choice: covered the eye of the land: spread over the land like a swarm
decisions.reason: The same words describe the locusts that covered Egypt (Exodus 10:5, 15). Balak pictures Israel as a swarm that leaves nothing behind (compare verse 4).

decisions.choice: the town of Pethor, the Euphrates River
decisions.reason: Readable names the river the Hebrew calls simply "the River" (see m2) and splits the long sentence.

decisions.choice: the eye of the land
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Hebrew picture, as in Exodus 10:5; Balanced says "the face of the land".

records.source: וְעַתָּה֩ לְכָה־נָּ֨א אָֽרָה־לִּ֜י אֶת־הָעָ֣ם הַזֶּ֗ה כִּֽי־עָצ֥וּם הוּא֙ מִמֶּ֔נִּי אוּלַ֤י אוּכַל֙ נַכֶּה־בּ֔וֹ וַאֲגָרְשֶׁ֖נּוּ מִן־הָאָ֑רֶץ כִּ֣י יָדַ֗עְתִּי אֵ֤ת אֲשֶׁר־תְּבָרֵךְ֙ מְבֹרָ֔ךְ וַאֲשֶׁ֥ר תָּאֹ֖ר יוּאָֽר׃
records.gloss: And now come, please, curse for me the people this, for mighty [is] it more than I; perhaps I will be able [that] we strike it and I drive it out from the land; for I know that whom you bless [is] blessed, and whom you curse is cursed.
pieces: So come now, please, and curse this people for me, because they are too strong for me. Perhaps then we will be able to defeat them, and I can drive them out of the land. For I know this: those you bless are blessed, and those you curse are cursed."

L.6: And now come, please, curse this people for me, for it [is] too mighty for me. Perhaps I will be able [so that] we may strike it, and I may drive it out of the land. For I know that whoever you bless [is] blessed, and whoever you curse is cursed."

R.6: Please come and curse these people for me. They are too strong for me. If you curse them, perhaps we will be able to defeat them, and I can drive them out of the land. I know that when you bless people, they are blessed. And when you curse people, they are cursed."

decisions.choice: curse: call down ruin by solemn words
decisions.reason: To curse was to speak words meant to bring harm on someone by calling on divine power. Balak wants Israel weakened before he fights them.

decisions.choice: perhaps I will be able, we may strike it: Balak with his army
decisions.reason: Balak speaks of himself ("I will be able", "I may drive it out"), but the verb for striking is "we". He means himself and his fighting men together. The mixed forms are kept.

decisions.choice: whoever you bless is blessed: Balak thinks the power lies in the seer's words
decisions.reason: Balak treats blessing and cursing as a power Balaam can sell. The story answers him: Balaam can say only what God puts in his mouth (verses 18, 38), and God had already said that those who bless Abraham's family will be blessed and those who curse it will be cursed (Genesis 12:3; Numbers 24:9).

decisions.choice: If you curse them
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that Balak's hope of winning rests on the curse, as the order of his words implies.

records.source: וַיֵּ֨לְכ֜וּ זִקְנֵ֤י מוֹאָב֙ וְזִקְנֵ֣י מִדְיָ֔ן וּקְסָמִ֖ים בְּיָדָ֑ם וַיָּבֹ֨אוּ֙ אֶל־בִּלְעָ֔ם וַיְדַבְּר֥וּ אֵלָ֖יו דִּבְרֵ֥י בָלָֽק׃
records.gloss: And went [the] elders of Moab and [the] elders of Midian, and divinations [were] in their hand; and they came to Balaam and spoke to him [the] words of Balak.
pieces: So the elders of Moab and of Midian set out, carrying the payment for divination. They came to Balaam and gave him Balak's message.

L.7: And the elders of Moab and the elders of Midian went, with [the fees for] divination in their hand; and they came to Balaam and spoke to him the words of Balak.

R.7: The elders of Moab and Midian left, taking money with them to pay Balaam for reading omens. They came to Balaam and told him what Balak had said.

decisions.choice: divinations in their hand: the fee for divination
decisions.reason: The word means divination, reading signs to learn what is hidden or what is coming. Carried "in their hand", it must mean the payment for it, as a gift was brought to a seer (1 Samuel 9:7-8). Israel's law forbids divination (Deuteronomy 18:10), and Joshua 13:22 calls Balaam "the diviner".

decisions.choice: the elders of Moab and of Midian: both peoples send envoys
decisions.reason: The two peoples act together, as in verse 4. From verse 8 on, the envoys are called Balak's "princes".

decisions.choice: [the fees for] divination
decisions.reason: Literal adds in brackets what the plain word means here (see m1).

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֲלֵיהֶ֗ם לִ֤ינוּ פֹה֙ הַלַּ֔יְלָה וַהֲשִׁבֹתִ֤י אֶתְכֶם֙ דָּבָ֔ר כַּאֲשֶׁ֛ר יְדַבֵּ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה אֵלָ֑י וַיֵּשְׁב֥וּ שָׂרֵֽי־מוֹאָ֖ב עִם־בִּלְעָֽם׃
records.gloss: And he said to them, lodge here the night, and I will bring back to you word as speaks YHWH to me. And stayed [the] princes of Moab with Balaam.
pieces: Balaam told them, "Stay here tonight. I will bring you a reply, just as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} tells it to me." So the officials of Moab stayed with Balaam.

L.8: And he said to them, "Lodge here tonight, and I will bring you back word, as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} speaks to me." And the princes of Moab stayed with Balaam.

R.8: Balaam said to them, "Stay here tonight. Then I will tell you what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says to me." So the leaders from Moab stayed with Balaam.

decisions.choice: as the LORD speaks to me: a foreign seer names Israel's God
decisions.reason: Balaam uses the divine name, YHWH. He claims to receive words from Israel's God, and the story shows the LORD really speaking to him, while it also shows that Balaam cannot make God serve his own ends (verses 12, 20, 22).

decisions.choice: lodge here tonight: waiting for word given at night
decisions.reason: God comes to Balaam at night (verses 9, 20), as he speaks to others in dreams by night (Genesis 20:3; 31:24). Balaam expects an answer by morning.

decisions.choice: princes: the king's high officials
decisions.reason: The word names men of rank who serve a king. These are the elders of verse 7, now seen as Balak's envoys.

decisions.choice: princes (L), officials (B), leaders (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the traditional "princes"; Balanced says "officials", since they are not the king's sons, and Readable says "leaders". The same words are used through the chapter.

records.source: וַיָּבֹ֥א אֱלֹהִ֖ים אֶל־בִּלְעָ֑ם וַיֹּ֕אמֶר מִ֛י הָאֲנָשִׁ֥ים הָאֵ֖לֶּה עִמָּֽךְ׃
records.gloss: And came God to Balaam and said, who [are] the men these with you?
pieces: God came to Balaam and asked, "Who are these men staying with you?"

L.9: And God came to Balaam and said, "Who [are] these men with you?"

R.9: That night God came to Balaam. He asked him, "Who are these men who are with you?"

decisions.choice: who are these men: a question that calls Balaam to account
decisions.reason: God does not ask because he does not know. As with Adam and Cain (Genesis 3:9; 4:9), the question makes Balaam say plainly what he is being asked to do.

decisions.choice: God: the narrator's word when God comes to Balaam
decisions.reason: In this chapter the narrator says "God" (Elohim) when God comes to Balaam (verses 9, 12, 20, 22), while Balaam speaks of "the LORD" (YHWH, verses 8, 13, 18-19), and the LORD acts in the story of the donkey (verses 22-35). Both name the one God of Israel.

decisions.choice: That night
decisions.reason: Readable says when God came, as verse 8 implies.

records.source: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר בִּלְעָ֖ם אֶל־הָאֱלֹהִ֑ים בָּלָ֧ק בֶּן־צִפֹּ֛ר מֶ֥לֶךְ מוֹאָ֖ב שָׁלַ֥ח אֵלָֽי׃
records.gloss: And said Balaam to God, Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, has sent to me,
pieces: Balaam answered God, "Balak son of Zippor, the king of Moab, has sent me this message,

L.10: And Balaam said to God, "Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, has sent [word] to me,

R.10: Balaam answered God, "Balak son of Zippor, the king of Moab, has sent me a message.

decisions.choice: has sent to me: the message follows
decisions.reason: The verb has no object; Balaam goes straight on to quote Balak's message in verse 11.

decisions.choice: [word] (L), this message (B), a message (R)
decisions.reason: English needs an object for "sent"; the levels supply what the next verse shows was sent.

records.source: הִנֵּ֤ה הָעָם֙ הַיֹּצֵ֣א מִמִּצְרַ֔יִם וַיְכַ֖ס אֶת־עֵ֣ין הָאָ֑רֶץ עַתָּ֗ה לְכָ֤ה קָֽבָה־לִּי֙ אֹת֔וֹ אוּלַ֥י אוּכַ֛ל לְהִלָּ֥חֶם בּ֖וֹ וְגֵרַשְׁתִּֽיו׃
records.gloss: Look, the people that came out from Egypt, and it covers the eye of the land; now come, curse for me it; perhaps I will be able to fight against it and I will drive it out.
pieces: 'The people that came out of Egypt are covering the face of the land. Come now and put a curse on them for me. Perhaps then I will be able to fight against them and drive them out.'"

L.11: 'Look, the people that has come out of Egypt, it has covered the eye of the land. Now come, put a curse on it for me. Perhaps I will be able to fight against it and drive it out.'"

R.11: He says, 'A nation has come out of Egypt, and they cover the land. Come now and curse them for me. Then perhaps I will be able to fight them and drive them away.'"

decisions.choice: put a curse on: a second word for cursing
decisions.reason: Balak's message in verse 6 used the common word for "curse" ('arar). Balaam, repeating it, uses another word (qabab) that also means to curse, perhaps by naming someone for ruin. It comes again in verse 17 and in 23:8, where Balaam asks how he can curse one whom God has not cursed.

decisions.choice: fight against it: Balaam retells the message in his own words
decisions.reason: Balaam leaves out "it is dwelling opposite me" and "whoever you bless is blessed" (verses 5-6), and says "fight against" where Balak said "strike". What Balak asks for is the same.

decisions.choice: put a curse on (L, B), curse (R)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced use a different English phrase for the second Hebrew word, so the reader can see the change (see m1); Readable says "curse" for both.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֱלֹהִים֙ אֶל־בִּלְעָ֔ם לֹ֥א תֵלֵ֖ךְ עִמָּהֶ֑ם לֹ֤א תָאֹר֙ אֶת־הָעָ֔ם כִּ֥י בָר֖וּךְ הֽוּא׃
records.gloss: And said God to Balaam, not you will go with them; not you will curse the people, for blessed [is] it.
pieces: But God said to Balaam, "You are not to go with them, nor are you to curse the people, because they are blessed."

L.12: And God said to Balaam, "You shall not go with them. You shall not curse the people, for it [is] blessed."

R.12: But God said to Balaam, "Do not go with these men. Do not curse the people of Israel, because I have blessed them."

decisions.choice: for it is blessed: Israel already stands under God's blessing
decisions.reason: God's answer is short and final. Israel is the people of the promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:2-3), and no seer's curse can undo what God has blessed (23:8, 20).

decisions.choice: You shall not: a firm prohibition
decisions.reason: "Not" with the plain future form states a firm rule, as in the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:13-15), not advice for one night.

decisions.choice: the people of Israel; I have blessed them
decisions.reason: Readable names the people and says who blessed them, since the blessing comes from God himself (Genesis 12:2; Numbers 23:20).

records.source: וַיָּ֤קָם בִּלְעָם֙ בַּבֹּ֔קֶר וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ אֶל־שָׂרֵ֣י בָלָ֔ק לְכ֖וּ אֶֽל־אַרְצְכֶ֑ם כִּ֚י מֵאֵ֣ן יְהוָ֔ה לְתִתִּ֖י לַהֲלֹ֥ךְ עִמָּכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And arose Balaam in the morning and said to [the] princes of Balak, go to your land, for has refused YHWH to let me go with you.
pieces: In the morning Balaam got up and said to Balak's officials, "Go back to your own country. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} will not allow me to go with you."

L.13: And Balaam rose in the morning and said to the princes of Balak, "Go to your land, for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has refused to let me go with you."

R.13: The next morning Balaam got up and said to Balak's leaders, "Go back home. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} will not let me go with you."

decisions.choice: the LORD has refused to let me go: Balaam tells only half of God's answer
decisions.reason: God said both "you shall not go" and "you shall not curse, for they are blessed" (verse 12). Balaam tells the envoys only that he may not go and says nothing of the blessing. That leaves room for Balak to try again with a larger offer (verses 15-17).

decisions.choice: Go back home
decisions.reason: "Go to your land" means returning home; Readable says it simply.

records.source: וַיָּק֨וּמוּ֙ שָׂרֵ֣י מוֹאָ֔ב וַיָּבֹ֖אוּ אֶל־בָּלָ֑ק וַיֹּ֣אמְר֔וּ מֵאֵ֥ן בִּלְעָ֖ם הֲלֹ֥ךְ עִמָּֽנוּ׃
records.gloss: And arose [the] princes of Moab and came to Balak and said, refuses Balaam to come with us.
pieces: So the officials of Moab set off, went back to Balak, and told him, "Balaam will not come with us."

L.14: And the princes of Moab rose and came to Balak and said, "Balaam refuses to come with us."

R.14: So the leaders from Moab went back to Balak. They told him, "Balaam would not come with us."

decisions.choice: Balaam refuses: the envoys do not say why
decisions.reason: Balaam said it was the LORD who refused (verse 13); the envoys report only that Balaam refused. So Balak thinks the problem is the price, and he raises it (verses 15-17).

records.source: וַיֹּ֥סֶף ע֖וֹד בָּלָ֑ק שְׁלֹ֣חַ שָׂרִ֔ים רַבִּ֥ים וְנִכְבָּדִ֖ים מֵאֵֽלֶּה׃
records.gloss: And again yet Balak sent princes, many and honored more than these.
pieces: Balak sent officials once more, more of them than before, and of higher rank than the first.

L.15: And Balak again sent princes, more numerous and more honored than these.

R.15: Then Balak sent other leaders. This time there were more of them, and they were more important than the first ones.

decisions.choice: more numerous and more honored: a greater embassy
decisions.reason: Sending more envoys, and men of higher rank, did Balaam greater honor and promised a greater reward (verse 17).

decisions.choice: again sent: literally "added again to send"
decisions.reason: The Hebrew uses "add" with another verb to say an action is repeated. The same verb returns in the donkey story, where Balaam strikes her "again" (verse 25) and the angel moves on "again" (verse 26).

records.source: וַיָּבֹ֖אוּ אֶל־בִּלְעָ֑ם וַיֹּ֣אמְרוּ ל֗וֹ כֹּ֤ה אָמַר֙ בָּלָ֣ק בֶּן־צִפּ֔וֹר אַל־נָ֥א תִמָּנַ֖ע מֵהֲלֹ֥ךְ אֵלָֽי׃
records.gloss: And they came to Balaam and said to him, thus says Balak son of Zippor, do not, please, be held back from coming to me,
pieces: They came to Balaam and said to him, "This is what Balak son of Zippor says: 'Please let nothing keep you from coming to me,

L.16: And they came to Balaam and said to him, "Thus says Balak son of Zippor: 'Please do not let [anything] hold you back from coming to me,

R.16: They came to Balaam and told him, "Balak son of Zippor says, 'Please do not let anything stop you from coming to me.

decisions.choice: Thus says: the words of a messenger
decisions.reason: Envoys spoke a king's words as if he were speaking, introduced by "thus says". The prophets use the same words for the message of the LORD.

decisions.choice: do not be held back: let nothing stop you
decisions.reason: The verb is passive: "do not let yourself be held back". Balak hints that something is keeping Balaam from coming and asks him not to give way to it.

decisions.choice: [anything]
decisions.reason: English needs a subject for "hold back"; Literal adds it in brackets.

records.source: כִּֽי־כַבֵּ֤ד אֲכַבֶּדְךָ֙ מְאֹ֔ד וְכֹ֛ל אֲשֶׁר־תֹּאמַ֥ר אֵלַ֖י אֶֽעֱשֶׂ֑ה וּלְכָה־נָּא֙ קָֽבָה־לִּ֔י אֵ֖ת הָעָ֥ם הַזֶּֽה׃
records.gloss: for honoring I will honor you greatly, and all that you say to me I will do; and come, please, curse for me the people this.
pieces: for I will give you great honor and do whatever you ask of me. Come, please, and put a curse on this people for me.'"

L.17: for I will greatly honor you, and all that you say to me I will do. So come, please, put a curse on this people for me.'"

R.17: I will reward you richly. I will do anything you ask. So please come and curse these people for me.'"

decisions.choice: honor: reward with wealth and high standing
decisions.reason: To "honor" someone here means to give him rich gifts and rank. Balaam hears it as silver and gold (verse 18), and Balak uses the word again in verse 37 and 24:11.

decisions.choice: I will greatly honor you: an emphatic promise
decisions.reason: The verb is doubled ("honoring I will honor") and "greatly" is added, to press the offer as hard as Balak can.

decisions.choice: put a curse on: the second word for cursing
decisions.reason: As in verse 11.

decisions.choice: reward you richly
decisions.reason: Readable says what the honor would be (see m1).

records.source: וַיַּ֣עַן בִּלְעָ֗ם וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ אֶל־עַבְדֵ֣י בָלָ֔ק אִם־יִתֶּן־לִ֥י בָלָ֛ק מְלֹ֥א בֵית֖וֹ כֶּ֣סֶף וְזָהָ֑ב לֹ֣א אוּכַ֗ל לַעֲבֹר֙ אֶת־פִּי֙ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהָ֔י לַעֲשׂ֥וֹת קְטַנָּ֖ה א֥וֹ גְדוֹלָֽה׃
records.gloss: And answered Balaam and said to [the] servants of Balak, if gives to me Balak [the] fullness of his house [of] silver and gold, not I am able to pass over the mouth of YHWH my God, to do small or great.
pieces: Balaam replied to Balak's officials, "Balak could give me his house filled with silver and gold, and still I could not do anything, small or great, that goes past what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} my God has said.

L.18: And Balaam answered and said to the servants of Balak, "If Balak were to give me his house full of silver and gold, I could not pass beyond the mouth of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} my God, to do [anything] small or great.

R.18: Balaam answered Balak's men, "Balak could give me his palace filled with silver and gold, and I still could not go against what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} my God commands, not even in the smallest thing.

decisions.choice: pass beyond the mouth of the LORD: act against what the LORD has said
decisions.reason: "The mouth" of the LORD is his spoken word or command (14:41; 24:13). To "pass beyond" it is to go further than it allows.

decisions.choice: the LORD my God: Balaam speaks as the LORD's own prophet
decisions.reason: Balaam claims Israel's God as his God. The story confirms that God speaks through him, yet it also shows his heart drawn to Balak's reward; later Scripture says he "loved the wages of wrongdoing" (2 Peter 2:15; compare Numbers 31:16).

decisions.choice: small or great: anything at all
decisions.reason: Naming the two extremes takes in everything between.

decisions.choice: servants (L), officials (B), men (R)
decisions.reason: These are Balak's envoys, the "princes" of verse 15, called the king's servants as officers of his court, as in Genesis 41:10. They were not owned slaves, so even Literal says "servants".

records.source: וְעַתָּ֗ה שְׁב֨וּ נָ֥א בָזֶ֛ה גַּם־אַתֶּ֖ם הַלָּ֑יְלָה וְאֵ֣דְעָ֔ה מַה־יֹּסֵ֥ף יְהוָ֖ה דַּבֵּ֥ר עִמִּֽי׃
records.gloss: And now stay, please, in this [place], also you, the night, and I will know what will add YHWH to speak with me.
pieces: Now you too, please, stay here tonight, so that I may learn what more {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has to say to me."

L.19: And now, please, stay here, you also, tonight, so that I may know what more {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will say to me."

R.19: But please stay here tonight, as the others did. Then I will find out if {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has anything more to tell me."

decisions.choice: what more the LORD will say: Balaam asks again after God has answered
decisions.reason: God had already said "You shall not go" and "You shall not curse" (verse 12). Asking again suggests that Balaam hopes for a different answer, with the reward in view; God's anger in verse 22 fits this. He may also mean only that he will not answer without God's word, as he says in verse 18.

decisions.choice: you also: like the first envoys
decisions.reason: "You also" looks back to the first envoys, who stayed the night in verse 8.

decisions.choice: as the others did
decisions.reason: Readable says what "you also" refers to (see m2).

records.source: וַיָּבֹ֨א אֱלֹהִ֥ים׀אֶל־בִּלְעָם֮ לַיְלָה֒ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר ל֗וֹ אִם־לִקְרֹ֤א לְךָ֙ בָּ֣אוּ הָאֲנָשִׁ֔ים ק֖וּם לֵ֣ךְ אִתָּ֑ם וְאַ֗ךְ אֶת־הַדָּבָ֛ר אֲשֶׁר־אֲדַבֵּ֥ר אֵלֶ֖יךָ אֹת֥וֹ תַעֲשֶֽׂה׃
records.gloss: And came God to Balaam [at] night and said to him, if to call you have come the men, arise, go with them; but only the word which I speak to you, it you will do.
pieces: God came to Balaam that night and said to him, "If the men have come to call you, then get up and go with them. But the word I give you, that and only that, you must do."

L.20: And God came to Balaam at night and said to him, "If the men have come to call you, rise, go with them; but only the word that I speak to you, that you shall do."

R.20: That night God came to Balaam. He said, "If these men have come to ask you to go with them, then go. But you must do only what I tell you to do."

decisions.choice: if the men have come to call you: since they have come
decisions.reason: "If" here states a fact that gives the reason: the men have indeed come. God now allows what he forbade in verse 12, but under a condition that keeps Balaam from cursing Israel.

decisions.choice: only the word that I speak: the condition of Balaam's going
decisions.reason: Balaam may go, but his words will not be his own. This is the rule of the whole story: the angel repeats it (verse 35), and Balaam says it himself (verse 38; 23:12, 26).

records.source: וַיָּ֤קָם בִּלְעָם֙ בַּבֹּ֔קֶר וַֽיַּחֲבֹ֖שׁ אֶת־אֲתֹנ֑וֹ וַיֵּ֖לֶךְ עִם־שָׂרֵ֥י מוֹאָֽב׃
records.gloss: And arose Balaam in the morning and saddled his donkey and went with [the] princes of Moab.
pieces: So in the morning Balaam got up, saddled his donkey, and set off with the officials of Moab.

L.21: And Balaam rose in the morning and saddled his donkey and went with the princes of Moab.

R.21: The next morning Balaam got up and put a saddle on his donkey. Then he left with the leaders from Moab.

decisions.choice: his donkey: a female donkey
decisions.reason: The word means a she-donkey, valued for riding (Judges 5:10). The verbs and pronouns for the donkey through the story are feminine, so she is "she" and "her".

decisions.choice: rose in the morning and saddled his donkey: words close to those used of Abraham
decisions.reason: Abraham too rose in the morning and saddled his donkey to go where God had told him (Genesis 22:3). Abraham went in obedience; Balaam goes with a reward in view. On each journey a messenger of the LORD meets the traveler on the way (Genesis 22:11; Numbers 22:22).

records.source: וַיִּֽחַר־אַ֣ף אֱלֹהִים֮ כִּֽי־הוֹלֵ֣ךְ הוּא֒ וַיִּתְיַצֵּ֞ב מַלְאַ֧ךְ יְהוָ֛ה בַּדֶּ֖רֶךְ לְשָׂטָ֣ן ל֑וֹ וְהוּא֙ רֹכֵ֣ב עַל־אֲתֹנ֔וֹ וּשְׁנֵ֥י נְעָרָ֖יו עִמּֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And burned [the] anger of God because going [was] he, and stationed himself [the] angel of YHWH in the road as an adversary to him; and he [was] riding on his donkey, and two of his young men [were] with him.
pieces: God's anger blazed up because Balaam was going, and the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} placed himself in the road to stand against him. Balaam was riding his donkey, with two of his servants beside him.

L.22: And the anger of God burned because he was going, and the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} took his stand in the road as an adversary to him. And he was riding on his donkey, and his two young men [were] with him.

R.22: But God was angry that Balaam went. So the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} stood in the road to stop him. Balaam was riding his donkey, and two of his servants were with him.

decisions.choice: God's anger burned because he was going, though God had allowed him to go
decisions.reason: God had just said "go with them" (verse 20), so his anger is surprising, and the text does not explain it. The rest of the story suggests that Balaam set out with his heart on Balak's reward, not only to speak God's word: the angel calls his way "reckless" (verse 32), and later Scripture says he "loved the wages of wrongdoing" (2 Peter 2:15-16). Read this way, God lets him go but stands against the way he goes. The text may also mean no more than that Balaam is to be taught, on the road, how fully he is in God's hands.

decisions.choice: the angel of the LORD: the LORD's messenger, who speaks with his authority
decisions.reason: "Angel" means messenger. Here the angel of the LORD says "the word that I speak to you" (verse 35), the same words God used in verse 20, and in other passages he speaks as God himself (Genesis 16:7-13; 22:11-12; Exodus 3:2-6). The text does not explain how the messenger and the LORD are related.

decisions.choice: as an adversary: one who stands in the way to oppose
decisions.reason: The word satan means an opponent or an obstacle. Here it is the angel's role, not a name: the LORD's own messenger blocks Balaam's road (verse 32).

decisions.choice: his two young men: Balaam's attendants
decisions.reason: The word means young men, and is often used of servants or attendants, as with the two who went with Abraham (Genesis 22:3). A man of rank traveled with servants.

decisions.choice: young men (L), servants (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the plain sense of the word; Balanced and Readable say what these young men were.

records.source: וַתֵּ֣רֶא הָאָתוֹן֩ אֶת־מַלְאַ֨ךְ יְהוָ֜ה נִצָּ֣ב בַּדֶּ֗רֶךְ וְחַרְבּ֤וֹ שְׁלוּפָה֙ בְּיָד֔וֹ וַתֵּ֤ט הָֽאָתוֹן֙ מִן־הַדֶּ֔רֶךְ וַתֵּ֖לֶךְ בַּשָּׂדֶ֑ה וַיַּ֤ךְ בִּלְעָם֙ אֶת־הָ֣אָת֔וֹן לְהַטֹּתָ֖הּ הַדָּֽרֶךְ׃
records.gloss: And saw the donkey the angel of YHWH standing in the road, and his sword drawn in his hand; and turned aside the donkey from the road and went into the field; and struck Balaam the donkey to turn her [back to] the road.
pieces: The donkey saw the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} standing in the road, his sword drawn and in his hand, and she left the road and went out into the field. Balaam struck her to bring her back to the road.

L.23: And the donkey saw the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} standing in the road, and his sword drawn in his hand; and the donkey turned aside from the road and went into the field. And Balaam struck the donkey to turn her [back to] the road.

R.23: The donkey saw the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} standing in the road. He had pulled out his sword and held it in his hand. So the donkey turned off the road and went into a field. Balaam hit the donkey to make her go back to the road.

decisions.choice: the donkey saw: the animal sees what the seer cannot
decisions.reason: Balaam is a famous seer, paid to see hidden things, yet his donkey sees the angel three times before he does (verses 23, 25, 27; then 31). The story turns his fame against him.

decisions.choice: his sword drawn in his hand: ready to kill
decisions.reason: A drawn sword shows that the angel has come to kill (verse 33). Joshua later meets the commander of the LORD's army with his sword drawn in his hand (Joshua 5:13).

decisions.choice: [back to] the road
decisions.reason: "To turn her the road" means to turn her back onto it; Literal adds the words in brackets.

records.source: וַֽיַּעֲמֹד֙ מַלְאַ֣ךְ יְהוָ֔ה בְּמִשְׁע֖וֹל הַכְּרָמִ֑ים גָּדֵ֥ר מִזֶּ֖ה וְגָדֵ֥ר מִזֶּֽה׃
records.gloss: And stood [the] angel of YHWH in a narrow path of the vineyards, a wall on this [side] and a wall on that [side].
pieces: Next the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} took his place where the path ran narrow among the vineyards, walled in on this side and on that.

L.24: And the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} stood in a narrow path of the vineyards, a wall on this [side] and a wall on that [side].

R.24: Then the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} stood where the path went between vineyards. There was a wall on each side of the path.

decisions.choice: a narrow path of the vineyards: a lane between walled fields
decisions.reason: Vineyards were fenced with walls of stones to keep animals out (Isaiah 5:5; Proverbs 24:31). A lane between two of them left no field to turn into, as there was in verse 23.

decisions.choice: walled in on this side and on that
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the Hebrew pattern of "a wall on this side and a wall on that side" in a shorter phrase.

records.source: וַתֵּ֨רֶא הָאָת֜וֹן אֶת־מַלְאַ֣ךְ יְהוָ֗ה וַתִּלָּחֵץ֙ אֶל־הַקִּ֔יר וַתִּלְחַ֛ץ אֶת־רֶ֥גֶל בִּלְעָ֖ם אֶל־הַקִּ֑יר וַיֹּ֖סֶף לְהַכֹּתָֽהּ׃
records.gloss: And saw the donkey the angel of YHWH and pressed herself against the wall and pressed [the] foot of Balaam against the wall; and he again struck her.
pieces: The donkey saw the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and pushed herself up against the wall, squeezing Balaam's foot against it, and he struck her once more.

L.25: And the donkey saw the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and she pressed herself against the wall and pressed Balaam's foot against the wall. And he struck her again.

R.25: When the donkey saw the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, she moved over against the wall. She crushed Balaam's foot against it. So Balaam hit her again.

decisions.choice: pressed herself, pressed Balaam's foot: the same verb twice
decisions.reason: The verb is used first of the donkey pressing herself to the wall and then of her pressing Balaam's foot. In moving away from the angel, she hurts her rider, and he strikes her for it.

decisions.choice: he struck her again: the second beating
decisions.reason: "Added to strike" means struck again, as Balak "added" to send in verse 15.

records.source: וַיּ֥וֹסֶף מַלְאַךְ־יְהוָ֖ה עֲב֑וֹר וַֽיַּעֲמֹד֙ בְּמָק֣וֹם צָ֔ר אֲשֶׁ֛ר אֵֽין־דֶּ֥רֶךְ לִנְט֖וֹת יָמִ֥ין וּשְׂמֹֽאול׃
records.gloss: And again passed on [the] angel of YHWH and stood in a narrow place where there [was] no way to turn right or left.
pieces: Once more the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} went on ahead. This time he stood in a tight spot with no way around him, right or left.

L.26: And the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} went on further and stood in a narrow place, where there was no way to turn to the right or to the left.

R.26: Then the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} went farther ahead. He stood in a place so narrow that the donkey could not get past him on either side.

decisions.choice: no way to turn right or left: no way of escape
decisions.reason: The three meetings grow tighter: first an open road beside a field (verse 23), then a walled lane (verse 24), now no room at all. Balaam is being hemmed in, as he will be when he tries three times to curse Israel (23:1-24:10).

decisions.choice: again passed on: moved ahead of them again
decisions.reason: "Added to pass on" means the angel moved on ahead once more, so as to meet them again.

decisions.choice: the donkey could not get past him on either side
decisions.reason: Readable says who could not turn aside: the donkey, as the next verse shows.

records.source: וַתֵּ֤רֶא הָֽאָתוֹן֙ אֶת־מַלְאַ֣ךְ יְהוָ֔ה וַתִּרְבַּ֖ץ תַּ֣חַת בִּלְעָ֑ם וַיִּֽחַר־אַ֣ף בִּלְעָ֔ם וַיַּ֥ךְ אֶת־הָאָת֖וֹן בַּמַּקֵּֽל׃
records.gloss: And saw the donkey the angel of YHWH and lay down under Balaam; and burned [the] anger of Balaam, and he struck the donkey with the staff.
pieces: The donkey saw the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and sank down under Balaam. Then Balaam's anger flared, and he struck the donkey with his staff.

L.27: And the donkey saw the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and lay down under Balaam. And Balaam's anger burned, and he struck the donkey with the staff.

R.27: This time when the donkey saw the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, she lay down with Balaam still on her back. Balaam became very angry, and he hit the donkey with his stick.

decisions.choice: Balaam's anger burned: the words used of God's anger in verse 22
decisions.reason: God's anger burned at Balaam (verse 22); now Balaam's anger burns at his donkey. He is angry with the one who is saving his life (verse 33).

decisions.choice: the staff: a stick for walking or for driving animals
decisions.reason: The word names a stick or rod, carried by travelers and herdsmen (Genesis 32:11).

decisions.choice: with Balaam still on her back
decisions.reason: Readable explains "under Balaam": she lay down while he was riding her.

records.source: וַיִּפְתַּ֥ח יְהוָ֖ה אֶת־פִּ֣י הָאָת֑וֹן וַתֹּ֤אמֶר לְבִלְעָם֙ מֶה־עָשִׂ֣יתִֽי לְךָ֔ כִּ֣י הִכִּיתַ֔נִי זֶ֖ה שָׁלֹ֥שׁ רְגָלִֽים׃
records.gloss: And opened YHWH the mouth of the donkey, and she said to Balaam, what have I done to you, that you have struck me these three times?
pieces: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} opened the donkey's mouth, and she said to Balaam, "What wrong have I done you, that you have struck me these three times?"

L.28: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} opened the mouth of the donkey, and she said to Balaam, "What have I done to you, that you have struck me these three times?"

R.28: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} made the donkey able to speak. She said to Balaam, "What have I done to you? Why have you hit me three times?"

decisions.choice: the LORD opened the mouth of the donkey: the LORD rules speech
decisions.reason: The LORD who makes an animal speak can also put his words in Balaam's mouth (verse 38; 23:5). 2 Peter 2:16 recalls that a donkey without speech spoke with a human voice and held back the prophet's madness.

decisions.choice: these three times: literally "these three feet"
decisions.reason: The word "foot" is used for a time or occurrence, as in "three times a year" (Exodus 23:14).

decisions.choice: made the donkey able to speak
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what "opened the mouth" means here.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר בִּלְעָם֙ לָֽאָת֔וֹן כִּ֥י הִתְעַלַּ֖לְתְּ בִּ֑י ל֤וּ יֶשׁ־חֶ֨רֶב֙ בְּיָדִ֔י כִּ֥י עַתָּ֖ה הֲרַגְתִּֽיךְ׃
records.gloss: And said Balaam to the donkey, because you have made a fool of me; if there were a sword in my hand, for now I would have killed you.
pieces: Balaam said to the donkey, "Because you have made me look a fool! If there were a sword in my hand, you would be dead already."

L.29: And Balaam said to the donkey, "Because you have made a fool of me! If there were a sword in my hand, I would have killed you by now."

R.29: Balaam told the donkey, "You have made me look stupid! If I had a sword with me, I would kill you on the spot!"

decisions.choice: made a fool of me: toyed with me, shamed me
decisions.reason: The verb is used of making sport of someone or dealing with them as one pleases (Exodus 10:2; 1 Samuel 31:4). Balaam feels shamed before his servants and Balak's princes.

decisions.choice: if there were a sword in my hand: an irony
decisions.reason: Balaam wishes for a sword, not seeing that the angel in front of him holds one, drawn, and that it is meant for him (verses 23, 33).

decisions.choice: You have made me look stupid! (no "because")
decisions.reason: Balaam's "because" answers the donkey's question directly, and Literal and Balanced keep it; Readable leaves it out, since it would not read naturally in plain English.

records.source: וַתֹּ֨אמֶר הָאָת֜וֹן אֶל־בִּלְעָ֗ם הֲלוֹא֩ אָנֹכִ֨י אֲתֹֽנְךָ֜ אֲשֶׁר־רָכַ֣בְתָּ עָלַ֗י מֵעֽוֹדְךָ֙ עַד־הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֔ה הַֽהַסְכֵּ֣ן הִסְכַּ֔נְתִּי לַעֲשׂ֥וֹת לְךָ֖ כֹּ֑ה וַיֹּ֖אמֶר לֹֽא׃
records.gloss: And said the donkey to Balaam, [am] not I your donkey on which you have ridden from your [lifetime] until this day? have I indeed been in the habit to do to you thus? And he said, no.
pieces: The donkey said to Balaam, "Am I not your own donkey? You have ridden me all your life, up to this very day. Was it ever my way to treat you like this?" "No," he answered.

L.30: And the donkey said to Balaam, "Am I not your donkey, on whom you have ridden all your life to this day? Have I ever been in the habit of doing so to you?" And he said, "No."

R.30: The donkey said to Balaam, "I am your own donkey. You have always ridden me, right up to today. Have I ever done anything like this to you before?" "No," Balaam said.

decisions.choice: from your lifetime until this day: for as long as you can remember
decisions.reason: The phrase means "ever since you have been". It need not be exact: the donkey has carried Balaam faithfully for a long time.

decisions.choice: have I ever been in the habit: a question expecting the answer no
decisions.reason: The verb is doubled for force, and Balaam must give the answer the question looks for: "No." Her past faithfulness shows that something must have stopped her.

decisions.choice: I am your own donkey
decisions.reason: Readable turns the question "Am I not ...?" into the statement it expects.

records.source: וַיְגַ֣ל יְהוָה֮ אֶת־עֵינֵ֣י בִלְעָם֒ וַיַּ֞רְא אֶת־מַלְאַ֤ךְ יְהוָה֙ נִצָּ֣ב בַּדֶּ֔רֶךְ וְחַרְבּ֥וֹ שְׁלֻפָ֖ה בְּיָד֑וֹ וַיִּקֹּ֥ד וַיִּשְׁתַּ֖חוּ לְאַפָּֽיו׃
records.gloss: And uncovered YHWH the eyes of Balaam, and he saw the angel of YHWH standing in the road and his sword drawn in his hand; and he bowed and prostrated himself to his face.
pieces: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} opened Balaam's eyes. Now he could see the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} standing in the road, his sword drawn and in his hand, and Balaam bowed his head and threw himself down, face to the ground.

L.31: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} uncovered the eyes of Balaam, and he saw the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} standing in the road, and his sword drawn in his hand; and he bowed his head and bowed down on his face.

R.31: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} let Balaam see. The angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} was standing in the road. He had pulled out his sword and held it in his hand. Balaam bowed down low with his face to the ground.

decisions.choice: uncovered the eyes: let him see what was hidden
decisions.reason: The verb means to uncover: the LORD takes away what kept Balaam from seeing. In his later sayings Balaam calls himself one whose eyes are uncovered (24:4, 16).

decisions.choice: bowed his head and bowed down: two signs of submission
decisions.reason: Bowing the head and then bowing to the ground was a way of showing honor and submission before a superior or before God (Genesis 24:26; Exodus 4:31).

decisions.choice: let Balaam see
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what "uncovered the eyes" means here.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֵלָיו֙ מַלְאַ֣ךְ יְהוָ֔ה עַל־מָ֗ה הִכִּ֨יתָ֙ אֶת־אֲתֹ֣נְךָ֔ זֶ֖ה שָׁל֣וֹשׁ רְגָלִ֑ים הִנֵּ֤ה אָנֹכִי֙ יָצָ֣אתִי לְשָׂטָ֔ן כִּֽי־יָרַ֥ט הַדֶּ֖רֶךְ לְנֶגְדִּֽי׃
records.gloss: And said to him [the] angel of YHWH, for what have you struck your donkey these three times? Look, I have come out as an adversary, because reckless [is your] way before me.
pieces: The angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to him, "Why have you struck your donkey these three times? It was I who came out to stand against you, because the way you are going is reckless in my sight.

L.32: And the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to him, "Why have you struck your donkey these three times? Look, I have come out as an adversary, because [your] way is reckless before me.

R.32: The angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} asked him, "Why did you hit your donkey three times? I came out to stand in your way, because what you are doing is reckless.

decisions.choice: your way is reckless: rushing headlong, or twisted
alternatives: your way is perverse before me
your way is evil before me
decisions.reason: The verb is rare. In Job 16:11 it seems to mean "throw headlong", so here it may describe Balaam's course as a rush toward ruin; others take it as "perverse" or "evil". Either way, the angel stands against the way Balaam has set out on (compare verse 22).

decisions.choice: why have you struck your donkey: the angel takes the donkey's part
decisions.reason: The angel's first words defend the donkey and so shame Balaam: the animal acted rightly and the seer did not.

decisions.choice: I have come out as an adversary: the role of verse 22
decisions.reason: The angel uses the word satan of himself, as the narrator did in verse 22: he came out to oppose Balaam, not to harm the donkey.

decisions.choice: It was I who came out
decisions.reason: Balanced brings out the stress on "I", which the Hebrew states with a separate pronoun after "Look".

records.source: וַתִּרְאַ֨נִי֙ הָֽאָת֔וֹן וַתֵּ֣ט לְפָנַ֔י זֶ֖ה שָׁלֹ֣שׁ רְגָלִ֑ים אוּלַי֙ נָטְתָ֣ה מִפָּנַ֔י כִּ֥י עַתָּ֛ה גַּם־אֹתְכָ֥ה הָרַ֖גְתִּי וְאוֹתָ֥הּ הֶחֱיֵֽיתִי׃
records.gloss: And saw me the donkey and turned aside before me these three times; if not she [had] turned aside from before me, surely now also you I would have killed and her I would have let live.
pieces: Three times the donkey saw me and swerved away from me. Had she not swerved away, I would have killed you by now, and kept her alive."

L.33: And the donkey saw me and turned aside before me these three times. If she had not turned aside from before me, surely by now I would have killed you and let her live."

R.33: Your donkey saw me and turned away three times. If she had not turned away, I would have killed you by now. But I would have let her live."

decisions.choice: if she had not turned aside: the donkey's turning saved him
alternatives: perhaps she turned aside from before me
decisions.reason: The word here usually means "perhaps". In this sentence it must mean "if not" or "unless", as the following "surely by now" shows.

decisions.choice: I would have killed you and let her live: the rescuer was the beast he beat
decisions.reason: Balaam wanted to kill the donkey (verse 29); the angel would have killed Balaam and spared the donkey. The animal he struck three times saved his life three times.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר בִּלְעָ֜ם אֶל־מַלְאַ֤ךְ יְהוָה֙ חָטָ֔אתִי כִּ֚י לֹ֣א יָדַ֔עְתִּי כִּ֥י אַתָּ֛ה נִצָּ֥ב לִקְרָאתִ֖י בַּדָּ֑רֶךְ וְעַתָּ֛ה אִם־רַ֥ע בְּעֵינֶ֖יךָ אָשׁ֥וּבָה לִּֽי׃
records.gloss: And said Balaam to [the] angel of YHWH, I have sinned, for not I knew that you [were] standing to meet me in the road; and now, if [it is] evil in your eyes, I will turn back for myself.
pieces: Balaam said to the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, "I have sinned. I did not know you were there in the road, standing to face me. Now, if this displeases you, I will turn back."

L.34: And Balaam said to the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, "I have sinned, for I did not know that you [were] standing to meet me in the road. And now, if [it is] evil in your eyes, I will turn back."

R.34: Balaam said to the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, "I have sinned. I did not know you were standing in the road to stop me. Now, if you do not want me to go on, I will go back home."

decisions.choice: I have sinned: a confession tied to what he did not know
decisions.reason: Balaam confesses that he was wrong, and gives as his reason that he did not know the angel was there. He offers to turn back only if the angel wishes it, though God's first answer had been plain (verse 12).

decisions.choice: evil in your eyes: displeasing to you
decisions.reason: "In someone's eyes" means in their judgment. "Evil in your eyes" means "wrong as you see it", "displeasing to you".

decisions.choice: to meet me: to confront me
decisions.reason: The phrase means "to meet" and is used of meeting in friendship or in battle. Here it means to oppose.

decisions.choice: go back home
decisions.reason: Readable says where Balaam would turn back to.

records.source: וַיֹּאמֶר֩ מַלְאַ֨ךְ יְהוָ֜ה אֶל־בִּלְעָ֗ם לֵ֚ךְ עִם־הָ֣אֲנָשִׁ֔ים וְאֶ֗פֶס אֶת־הַדָּבָ֛ר אֲשֶׁר־אֲדַבֵּ֥ר אֵלֶ֖יךָ אֹת֣וֹ תְדַבֵּ֑ר וַיֵּ֥לֶךְ בִּלְעָ֖ם עִם־שָׂרֵ֥י בָלָֽק׃
records.gloss: And said [the] angel of YHWH to Balaam, go with the men; but only the word which I speak to you, it you shall speak. And went Balaam with [the] princes of Balak.
pieces: The angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to Balaam, "Go on with the men. But the word I give you, that and only that, you are to speak." So Balaam went on with Balak's officials.

L.35: And the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to Balaam, "Go with the men, but only the word that I speak to you, that you shall speak." And Balaam went with the princes of Balak.

R.35: The angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to Balaam, "Go with the men. But you must say only what I tell you to say." So Balaam went on with Balak's leaders.

decisions.choice: only the word that I speak to you: God's condition of verse 20, now about speaking
decisions.reason: The angel repeats God's words of verse 20 almost exactly, but "you shall do" becomes "you shall speak". The danger was in what Balaam would say over Israel. The angel speaks here with God's own words (see the note on verse 22).

decisions.choice: Balaam went with the princes of Balak: the journey goes on
decisions.reason: The story returns to where verse 21 left it; what follows takes place in Moab.

records.source: וַיִּשְׁמַ֥ע בָּלָ֖ק כִּ֣י בָ֣א בִלְעָ֑ם וַיֵּצֵ֨א לִקְרָאת֜וֹ אֶל־עִ֣יר מוֹאָ֗ב אֲשֶׁר֙ עַל־גְּב֣וּל אַרְנֹ֔ן אֲשֶׁ֖ר בִּקְצֵ֥ה הַגְּבֽוּל׃
records.gloss: And heard Balak that had come Balaam, and he went out to meet him to [the] city of Moab, which [is] on [the] border of Arnon, which [is] at [the] edge of the territory.
pieces: News reached Balak that Balaam was on his way, and he went out to meet him at the city of Moab, which stands on the Arnon border at the very edge of the territory.

L.36: And Balak heard that Balaam had come, and he went out to meet him at the city of Moab, which [is] on the border of the Arnon, which [is] at the edge of the territory.

R.36: Balak heard that Balaam was on his way. So he went out to meet him at the city of Moab. This city was by the Arnon River, at the edge of Balak's land.

decisions.choice: the city of Moab: perhaps Ar of Moab
decisions.reason: The words may name a particular town, perhaps the Ar of Moab named beside the Arnon in 21:15, 28. Balak goes to the far edge of his land to receive his guest, an honor in itself.

decisions.choice: the Arnon: the deep valley on Moab's northern border
decisions.reason: The Arnon flows west into the Dead Sea through a deep gorge. It was the border between Moab and the Amorites (21:13, 26).

decisions.choice: the Arnon River, Balak's land
decisions.reason: Readable says what the Arnon is and whose territory is meant.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר בָּלָ֜ק אֶל־בִּלְעָ֗ם הֲלֹא֩ שָׁלֹ֨חַ שָׁלַ֤חְתִּי אֵלֶ֨יךָ֙ לִקְרֹא־לָ֔ךְ לָ֥מָּה לֹא־הָלַ֖כְתָּ אֵלָ֑י הַֽאֻמְנָ֔ם לֹ֥א אוּכַ֖ל כַּבְּדֶֽךָ׃
records.gloss: And said Balak to Balaam, did I not indeed send to you to call you? Why did you not come to me? Am I really not able to honor you?
pieces: Balak said to Balaam, "I sent for you with such urgency! Why did you not come to me? Did you think I could not pay you what you are worth?"

L.37: And Balak said to Balaam, "Did I not urgently send to you to call you? Why did you not come to me? Am I really not able to honor you?"

R.37: Balak said to Balaam, "I sent you an urgent message to come! Why did you not come? Did you think I could not reward you well?"

decisions.choice: did I not urgently send: a doubled verb
decisions.reason: The verb "send" is doubled for force, as "honor" is in verse 17. Balak stresses how much he wanted Balaam.

decisions.choice: honor: reward with wealth and rank
decisions.reason: As in verse 17. Balak still thinks the delay was about the price.

decisions.choice: why did you not come to me: Balak's complaint
decisions.reason: Balak heard only that Balaam refused (verse 14), so he takes the delay as bargaining, not as God's refusal.

decisions.choice: pay you what you are worth (B), reward you well (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what Balak's honor would be, as in verse 17; Literal keeps "honor".

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר בִּלְעָ֜ם אֶל־בָּלָ֗ק הִֽנֵּה־בָ֨אתִי֙ אֵלֶ֔יךָ עַתָּ֕ה הֲיָכ֥וֹל אוּכַ֖ל דַּבֵּ֣ר מְא֑וּמָה הַדָּבָ֗ר אֲשֶׁ֨ר יָשִׂ֧ים אֱלֹהִ֛ים בְּפִ֖י אֹת֥וֹ אֲדַבֵּֽר׃
records.gloss: And said Balaam to Balak, look, I have come to you; now, am I at all able to speak anything? The word that puts God in my mouth, it I will speak.
pieces: Balaam replied, "Here I am; I have come to you. But can I say just anything now? The word God places in my mouth, that is what I will speak."

L.38: And Balaam said to Balak, "Look, I have come to you. Now, am I at all able to speak anything? The word that God puts in my mouth, that I will speak."

R.38: Balaam answered, "I am here now. But I cannot say whatever I want. I can say only the words God gives me to say."

decisions.choice: am I at all able to speak anything: a question expecting no
decisions.reason: The verb "be able" is doubled. Balaam means that he has no power to say anything of his own.

decisions.choice: puts in my mouth: gives me the words to speak
decisions.reason: The phrase is used of God giving words to a prophet (Deuteronomy 18:18; Jeremiah 1:9). The LORD does this to Balaam in 23:5, 16.

decisions.choice: I cannot say whatever I want
decisions.reason: Readable turns the question into the statement it expects.

records.source: וַיֵּ֥לֶךְ בִּלְעָ֖ם עִם־בָּלָ֑ק וַיָּבֹ֖אוּ קִרְיַ֥ת חֻצֽוֹת׃
records.gloss: And went Balaam with Balak, and they came [to] Kiriath-huzoth.
pieces: Then Balaam went with Balak, and they came to Kiriath-huzoth.

L.39: And Balaam went with Balak, and they came [to] Kiriath-huzoth.

R.39: Balaam went with Balak to the town of Kiriath-huzoth.

decisions.choice: Kiriath-huzoth: "town of streets", a town in Moab
decisions.reason: The name means "town of streets" or "town of open places". Its site is not known.

decisions.choice: the town of
decisions.reason: Readable says that Kiriath-huzoth is a town.

records.source: וַיִּזְבַּ֥ח בָּלָ֖ק בָּקָ֣ר וָצֹ֑אן וַיְשַׁלַּ֣ח לְבִלְעָ֔ם וְלַשָּׂרִ֖ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר אִתּֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And sacrificed Balak cattle and sheep, and sent to Balaam and to the princes who [were] with him.
pieces: Balak sacrificed cattle and sheep and sent some of the meat to Balaam and to the officials who were with him.

L.40: And Balak sacrificed cattle and sheep, and sent [portions] to Balaam and to the princes who [were] with him.

R.40: Balak offered cattle and sheep as sacrifices. He sent some of the meat to Balaam and to the leaders who were with him.

decisions.choice: sacrificed and sent: a sacrificial meal for the guests
decisions.reason: In a sacrifice of this kind most of the meat was eaten by the worshipers and their guests (compare Exodus 18:12). Sending portions honored Balaam and those with him. The text does not say to which god Balak sacrificed.

decisions.choice: [portions] (L), some of the meat (B, R)
decisions.reason: The verb "sent" has no object; what was sent was the meat of the sacrifice.

records.source: וַיְהִ֣י בַבֹּ֔קֶר וַיִּקַּ֤ח בָּלָק֙ אֶת־בִּלְעָ֔ם וַֽיַּעֲלֵ֖הוּ בָּמ֣וֹת בָּ֑עַל וַיַּ֥רְא מִשָּׁ֖ם קְצֵ֥ה הָעָֽם׃
records.gloss: And it was in the morning, and took Balak Balaam and brought him up [to] Bamoth-baal, and he saw from there [the] edge of the people.
pieces: The next morning Balak took Balaam and brought him up to Bamoth-baal. From there Balaam could see the outer edge of the people.

L.41: And it was in the morning, and Balak took Balaam and brought him up [to] Bamoth-baal, and from there he saw the edge of the people.

R.41: The next morning Balak took Balaam up to Bamoth-baal, which means "the high places of Baal." From there Balaam could see some of the Israelites at the edge of their camp.

decisions.choice: Bamoth-baal: "high places of Baal", a height in Moab
decisions.reason: The name means the "heights" or "high places" of Baal, the Canaanite storm god. Such hilltops were places of worship. Israel had passed a place called Bamoth on its way (21:19-20), perhaps the same.

decisions.choice: the edge of the people: part of Israel's camp, not all of it
alternatives: the whole people, to its farthest part
decisions.reason: The word can mean the near or the far edge of something. In 23:13 Balak says that Balaam saw "only its edge" and not all of it, so here it means only part of the camp. Balak seems to think that the seer must see the people he curses.

decisions.choice: which means "the high places of Baal"; some of the Israelites at the edge of their camp
decisions.reason: Readable explains the name and says what "the edge of the people" was.
